sentences.text: Ankylosaurus is possibly the largest known ankylosaurid, with an estimated length of 6 to 8 meters and a weight of 4.8 to 8 metric tons.
It is also considered the largest known ankylosaurine dinosaur and possibly the largest ankylosaurid overall.
The skull was low, triangular, and wider than it was long, featuring a broad and low back.
This quadrupedal dinosaur had hind limbs that were longer than its forelimbs.
Its body was protected by distinctive armor made of bone knobs and plates called osteoderms embedded in its skin.
These thin osteoderms were reinforced by randomly distributed cushions of collagen fibers embedded directly into the bone tissue.
The tail club served as an active defensive weapon capable of breaking the bones of an attacker.
The animal likely weighed around 6 tons.
It became the best-known ankylosaur in popular culture, possibly due to a life-sized reconstruction at the 1964 World's Fair in New York City.
A 2009 study showed that large tail clubs could generate enough force to break bones during impacts, but medium and small ones could not.
The genus Ankylosaurus was named by Barnum Brown in 1908.
The genus was established by Brown in 1908.
The type specimen of Ankylosaurus magniventris was discovered in 1906 by Barnum Brown in the Hell Creek Formation near Gilbert Creek, Montana.
The type specimen comes from the Hell Creek Formation in Montana, with other fossils found in Wyoming, Alberta, and Saskatchewan.
Only a few Ankylosaurus specimens have been found, and no complete skeleton has been discovered yet.
Ankylosaurus was a herbivore, like other ornithischian dinosaurs.
It likely fed as a non-selective browser, indicated by its broad muzzle.
Partially ossified and inelastic tail tendons allowed great force to be transmitted to the tail club.
The U-shaped zygapophyses and neural spines of tail vertebrae differ from the V-shape of most other ankylosaurids, possibly due to a wider tail handle.
The tail club was semicircular from above, distinguishing it from the pointed clubs of Anodontosaurus and the narrow clubs of Dyoplosaurus.
Coombs suggested ankylosaurs may have been capable diggers, though limited by their hoof-like hands.
The blunter squamosal horns in larger specimens compared to smaller ones may represent ontogenetic variation.
In 1977, Teresa Maryańska proposed ankylosaur sinuses may have lightened the skull, housed a gland, or aided vocal resonance.
Ankylosaurus belongs to the family Ankylosauridae, with Anodontosaurus and Euoplocephalus as its closest relatives.
Henry Fairfield Osborn named the suborder Ankylosauria in 1923.
Ankylosaurus lived between 68 and 66 million years ago during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous Period.
It likely inhabited upland areas, as its ecological niche did not overlap with the nodosaurid Denversaurus.
The clade Thyreophora, which includes Ankylosaurus, existed from the Sinemurian age until the Maastrichtian, spanning 135 million years.
The rarity of fossils suggests it was ecologically rare or restricted to uplands where fossilization was less likely.
In 2015, Arbour and Currie disputed Carpenter's interpretation of cervical armor, noting the holotype fragments did not fit his proposed arrangement, though breakage might explain the discrepancy.
In 1969, Georg Haas concluded that ankylosaur skull musculature was relatively weak despite the large skull size.
Carpenter rejected the idea that ankylosaur sinuses aided vocalization or significantly reduced skull weight.
